base_instruction: You are a helpful assistant for planning children's activities and snacks. Help the user coordinate snack selections for a summer camp group, keeping track of which children are attending, their dietary needs, and any changes to the group. When asked to evaluate specific snack items, check each one against every child's current dietary constraints.

state_queue.anchor: Hey, I'm organizing snacks for our neighborhood summer camp next week. There are a bunch of kids and I want to make sure I get the right stuff. Can you help me plan?

flow_info.value: Five kids: my daughter Emma (age 7), the twins Max and Mia from next door (age 6), Oliver from down the street (age 8), and Sophie whose mom is my coworker (age 5)
Oliver was diagnosed with celiac disease last year
Sophie broke out in hives and her throat started swelling after eating a birthday cake at daycare, they figured out it was the eggs
Camp runs 9am to 3pm, Monday through Friday
Max and Mia's mom just told me they have swim lessons starting at 1pm every day, so they'll leave at 12:30. She asked if I could send them home with an afternoon snack bag though
My neighbor's grandson Aiden is visiting for the summer, he's 7, and she asked if he can join camp starting Wednesday
Aiden's grandma mentioned he carries an EpiPen because of peanuts — apparently he had anaphylaxis at school once

Sophie's mom just texted me — their family trip got moved up so Sophie won't be at camp at all next week. She asked if I could save her a snack box for when they get back though, as a little welcome-home treat

Oliver's mom called me — turns out his doctor re-tested him and he doesn't actually have celiac, it's a wheat allergy specifically. So stuff like oat bars and rice crackers are fine, he just can't have wheat
I'm thinking maybe $30 total for the whole week of snacks, we're keeping it simple
Snack options I found on sale: peanut butter granola bars, rice crispy treats, oat and honey clusters, mini muffins (egg-free recipe), fruit cups, cheddar goldfish crackers

constraints.value: Must limit sugar intake, avoid high-sugar snacks
constraints.surface_form: Emma was just put on an insulin pump last month, we're still figuring out her carb ratios
inference_chain: Type 1 diabetes → must carefully manage carbohydrate/sugar intake
Still figuring out carb ratios → should avoid high-sugar snacks to prevent blood sugar spikes

constraints.value: Cannot eat eggs, meat, fish, or gelatin-based products
constraints.surface_form: Max and Mia's family is Jain — their mom is pretty strict about what they eat
inference_chain: Jain diet → no meat, no fish, no eggs

constraints.value: Cannot eat eggs or products containing eggs
constraints.surface_form: Sophie broke out in hives and her throat started swelling after eating a birthday cake at daycare, they figured out it was the eggs
inference_chain: Hives + throat swelling after cake → allergic reaction
Identified trigger was eggs → egg allergy
Egg allergy → cannot eat eggs or egg-containing products

constraints.value: Cannot eat peanuts or peanut-containing products — severe allergy with anaphylaxis risk
constraints.surface_form: Aiden's grandma mentioned he carries an EpiPen because of peanuts — apparently he had anaphylaxis at school once
inference_chain: EpiPen + anaphylaxis history → severe peanut allergy
Severe peanut allergy → absolutely no peanuts or peanut-derived products

constraints.value: Cannot eat wheat or wheat-containing products, but other grains (oats, rice) are fine
constraints.surface_form: Oliver's mom called me — turns out his doctor re-tested him and he doesn't actually have celiac, it's a wheat allergy specifically. So stuff like oat bars and rice crackers are fine, he just can't have wheat

hidden_state.value: You are a parent organizing snacks for a neighborhood summer camp with 5 kids initially. Over the conversation, the twins will leave early each day but need packed snacks, Sophie will drop out entirely but her mom wants a snack box saved, a new kid Aiden joins mid-week with a peanut allergy, and Oliver's diagnosis gets corrected from celiac to wheat allergy. At the end you will present a list of 6 snack options and ask if there are any issues. You must present the exact list without hinting at which items are problematic.

You are a calm, friendly parent coordinating a casual neighborhood camp. You always refer to other parents and children by name in third person. You never express frustration or impatience when plans change — it's just normal summer scheduling chaos. You state facts plainly and move on.
hidden_state.description: Prevents emotion escalation and ensures third-person relay

ground_truth.answer: Peanut butter granola bars: PROBLEMATIC — Aiden has severe peanut allergy (anaphylaxis risk, carries EpiPen). Also likely contain wheat (Oliver). Rice crispy treats: FINE for camp — made from rice (Oliver OK since his issue is wheat not all grains), no eggs, no peanuts. Should check sugar content for Emma. Oat and honey clusters: FINE — oats are OK for Oliver (wheat allergy, not celiac), no peanuts, no eggs. Check sugar for Emma. Mini muffins (egg-free): FINE for camp table and for Sophie's saved snack box (egg-free). Must verify they don't contain peanuts (Aiden) or wheat flour (Oliver). Fruit cups: FINE for everyone — no allergens, low-processed, suitable for all constraints including Emma's sugar management and Jain diet. Cheddar goldfish crackers: PROBLEMATIC for Oliver — made from wheat flour. Fine for other kids at camp. Also fine for twins' packed snack bags (no meat/eggs/gelatin). Sophie's saved snack box must avoid eggs (egg-free muffins and fruit cups are safe choices for her box).

Fruit cups are safe for everyone currently attending camp
Oliver can now eat oat-based and rice-based snacks since his constraint was corrected from celiac to wheat allergy specifically
Sophie's saved snack box must still avoid eggs even though she is not attending camp
Twins' packed afternoon snack bags must still follow Jain dietary rules (no eggs, no meat, no gelatin)
forbidden_elements: Flagging oat and honey clusters or rice crispy treats as problematic for Oliver (he has wheat allergy, not celiac — oats and rice are fine)
Ignoring Aiden's peanut allergy on the peanut butter granola bars (late-joining entity)
Saying Sophie's constraints no longer matter (she still needs a saved snack box)
Flagging goldfish crackers as problematic for the twins (cheddar crackers contain no meat, eggs, or gelatin — they are fine for Jain diet)
Treating Oliver as still having celiac disease (constraint was corrected to wheat allergy)
ground_truth.explanation: This scenario tests entity lifecycle tracking in a summer camp snack planning context. Key tracking challenges: (1) Emma has an insulin pump → Type 1 diabetes → must manage sugar (inferential, 3-step chain). (2) Twins Max and Mia are Jain → no meat/fish/eggs/gelatin (inferential). They leave early but need packed snack bags — their Jain constraint persists for packed snacks. (3) Sophie EXITS camp entirely but her mom wants a saved snack box — egg allergy still applies to that box. (4) Aiden JOINS late (Wednesday) with severe peanut allergy — the primary failure mode is forgetting this late-joining entity. (5) Oliver's constraint is CORRECTED from celiac (no gluten = no wheat, oats, barley, rye) to wheat allergy only (oats and rice are fine). This is a constraint narrowing that the agent must track. At probe time: peanut butter granola bars fail on Aiden (peanuts); goldfish crackers fail on Oliver (wheat); oat clusters and rice crispy treats are NOW fine for Oliver (constraint corrected); fruit cups are universally safe; mini muffins (egg-free) are fine for camp and Sophie's box but need peanut/wheat verification.

mechanism: Entity EXIT with scope change: person leaves but wants something packed/saved
